canDo: Can read 350–500-word informative articles on science or society using the method “title → paragraph gist → locate the question → check the text”, and rule out plausible-looking distractors in pick-1-of-3 questions.
review: Review the passive (être + past participle, se faire / se voir + infinitive) and nominalisation (-tion, -ment, -age, -ure), the most common written features of informative articles and news headlines; also look back at the listening location strategies from days 29–30.
input: Read: a long report on “participatory science”, a column on science and public opinion and an announcement for a volunteer river-monitoring project; read the questions first, then read closely, underlining passive sentences and nominalisations. Listen: an interview with an astrophysicist and science communicator, a column on “how to read health statistics” and a news flash on trust in science.
output: Write: an article of 250+ words for a university newspaper presenting the advantages and limits of participatory science, with at least 3 passive sentences and 3 nominalisations; speak: a 6-minute monologue on “should scientists take part in public debate?”, then handle 4 counter-arguments from the examiner in the debate.
checkpoint: At least 5/6 correct on R31-1, pointing to the evidence in the text for each; can rewrite 5 verb phrases as nominalised headlines; a 6-minute monologue with a clear problem statement and an announced two-part structure.
challenge: Today’s challenge: find a news item about scientific research on RFI’s « Journal en français facile » or TV5MONDE, copy out 3 passive sentences or nominalised headlines, then write 3 sentences giving your own view with today’s expressions (e.g. « Cette découverte a été rendue possible grâce à… »).

questions.why: The article covers, in turn, the definition, history, advantages (scale of data), reliability issues and potential biases of participatory science: it is a comprehensive overview. A picks up only the “reliability” paragraph and is too strong; C: the app is just an example, and the article doesn’t aim to call readers to action.

The text says « Le phénomène n’est pas nouveau… Mais la diffusion des smartphones a permis de changer d’échelle »: what is new is the scale. B and C are exactly what the text says is “not new” (« Depuis longtemps, des relevés… sont effectués par des observateurs bénévoles »).

The quote « Aucun laboratoire ne pourrait financer la surveillance de milliers de sites pendant dix ans » points directly to scale and cost. A contradicts the fourth paragraph (beginners often misidentify species); B isn’t mentioned.

The text: « les observations douteuses sont systématiquement vérifiées par des spécialistes » and « c’est l’accumulation de milliers de relevés qui permet de dégager des tendances ». A: the text sets no entry restrictions; C exaggerates: only “doubtful” observations are checked, not “every one”.

dégager here means “to bring out, to reveal”, and tendances means “overall trends”. B misreads dégager as “to clear away”; C is the opposite of the context: a single observation is worth little; it takes large amounts of data.

« les volontaires ne doivent pas être considérés comme une main-d’œuvre gratuite destinée à compenser la baisse des financements publics ». A and C don’t appear in the text; they are common-sense guesses used as distractors.

The core argument is in paragraphs four and five: « C’est donc à l’école que tout se joue… en enseignant comment une connaissance est produite ». B is the position the author explicitly rejects (« je ne réclame pas la soumission aveugle aux experts »); A isn’t argued in the text.

« l’avis d’une chercheuse… est mis sur le même plan que celui d’un polémiste », i.e. giving equal weight to opinions of unequal value and thereby “manufacturing false debates”. B and C aren’t mentioned.
« ce doute obéit à des règles : il s’appuie sur des données… il accepte d’être contredit. Le soupçon généralisé, lui, ne repose sur rien ». A is a wrong inference; C: the text compares no age groups.

se nourrir de = to feed on; ouverture = openness (open access, public discussion). The author calls it a paradoxe: the more transparent science is, the more the public sees its “hesitations”, and the less it trusts it. B is the exact opposite; A gets the subject wrong.

« L’exigence est plus haute, mais c’est la seule qui protège… »: it admits the bar is higher but offers a way forward, so the tone is demanding yet positive. B doesn’t fit: the author isn’t disillusioned or sarcastic; C doesn’t fit: the ending takes a clear stance.

« Communiqué » and « annonce le lancement des… » show it is the association’s project announcement. A: the text reports no specific pollution incident; C: participants « ne percevront aucune rémunération », so it isn’t a job ad.

« chaque binôme relèvera la température et le niveau de l’eau, photographiera les berges et signalera toute anomalie ». A is wrong: the passive « Leur analyse sera assurée par l’équipe universitaire » shows the university team does the analysis; B isn’t mentioned.

« seuls les services de l’État sont habilités à intervenir. Le rôle des volontaires est de donner l’alerte, non de mener l’enquête ». B contradicts “only state services are authorised to intervene”; C isn’t mentioned.

« Priorité sera donnée aux habitants des communes riveraines et aux personnes pouvant s’engager pour une année complète ». Neither A nor C is a condition in the announcement (equipment and training are provided by the project).

The whole interview is about why she makes science videos, whether institutions recognise this work and how far to simplify. A is only the topic of her first school talk; C: the lab’s financial difficulties aren’t discussed.

« j’ai été frappée par la curiosité des élèves… ils n’avaient aucun endroit où trouver des réponses à la fois fiables et accessibles ». She says « sans grande ambition », which rules out B; A contradicts the fact that her lab doesn’t recognise the work.

« une carrière de chercheur est évaluée presque uniquement sur les publications. Les heures passées à préparer une vidéo ne sont prises en compte nulle part ». B goes too far: officially, sharing knowledge is even part of their mission; C isn’t mentioned.
« je découvre souvent des points que je n’avais pas vraiment compris moi-même ». A mixes in the “public money” argument; C: she doesn’t say her colleagues were convinced.
« on a le droit de simplifier, mais pas de dire quelque chose de faux ». A is too absolute: she can discuss hypotheses, as long as she doesn’t present them as a fait établi; B isn’t mentioned.
« ils créent des attentes qui seront forcément déçues. À long terme, c’est la confiance du public qui en souffre ». B and C are unfounded guesses.

The column explains two “traps” (relative risk; correlation ≠ causation) and suggests two questions to ask yourself, helping listeners treat the numbers in news reports with care. A is only the example in the title; C: he criticises how numbers are presented, not researchers.
The set phrase y perdre son latin = to be baffled, not to know what to make of it: one study says one thing today, another seems to say the opposite tomorrow. B and C are literal misreadings.

A 50% increase on “2 in 10,000” only makes “3 in 10,000”: « L’augmentation est réelle, mais elle est très loin de ce que le titre laisse imaginer ». A confuses relative and absolute risk; B: he doesn’t dismiss the study itself.

It comes right after « confondre corrélation et causalité »: dog owners see the doctor less, perhaps because they were healthier to begin with or walk more. B is exactly the conclusion he wants to avoid; C: the example is about dog owners, not animal experiments.
« posez-vous deux questions : combien de personnes sont réellement concernées, et le lien est-il prouvé ou seulement observé ? ». A is too extreme; B isn’t what he suggests.
« cette confiance varie fortement selon les domaines »: high in medicine and astronomy, low for food and artificial intelligence. A is the opposite; C: AI is precisely an area of low trust.
« seuls 20 % d’entre eux disent vérifier la source… avant de la partager ». B isn’t mentioned; C is the opposite of « s’informent d’abord sur les réseaux sociaux ».
« les laboratoires de l’université seront exceptionnellement ouverts au public vendredi soir, jusqu’à minuit ». A and B attach details from the earlier news items to this one.

V31-01.zh: to bring to light, to reveal
V31-01.exZh: Volunteers’ records have revealed the decline of several species.

V31-02.exZh: Volunteers mostly take part in data collection, rarely in data analysis.

V31-03.zh: to scale up, to change scale
V31-03.exZh: Thanks to smartphones, these projects scaled up within a few years.

V31-04.exZh: Only thousands of accumulated records make it possible to identify reliable trends.

V31-05.exZh: To correct identification errors, the protocols were simplified.

V31-06.exZh: Several researchers warn against exploiting volunteers.

V31-07.exZh: Volunteers should not become free labour for laboratories.

V31-08.zh: the scientific method, the scientific process
V31-08.exZh: Taking part in an observation helps you understand the scientific process: question, protocol, interpretation.

V31-09.zh: to put on the same level
V31-09.exZh: You can’t put expert opinion on the same level as rumours.

V31-10.exZh: Before publication, every paper goes through peer review.

V31-11.exZh: Public distrust feeds on contradictions between experts.

V31-12.exZh: More and more studies are published open-access online.

V31-13.exZh: Concluding that “dogs cure their owners” confuses correlation with causation.

V31-14.zh: to enter the fray, to join public debate
V31-14.exZh: After long keeping a low profile, many climate scientists eventually entered the fray.

V31-15.zh: in the name of, under the banner of
V31-15.exZh: In the name of “balance”, some media manufacture controversy.

V31-16.exZh: Officially, sharing knowledge is part of researchers’ mission.

V31-17.exZh: A good science communicator explains without oversimplifying.

V31-18.exZh: This hypothesis is interesting, but it isn’t an established fact yet.

V31-19.exZh: Sensational headlines raise expectations that are bound to be disappointed.

V31-20.zh: to be baffled, not to know what to make of it
V31-20.exZh: One study says yes, another says no: people end up baffled.

V31-21.exZh: A single study is never enough to establish a scientific conclusion.

V31-22.exZh: The author recommends strengthening media literacy education from secondary school onwards.

V31-23.zh: to be set up, to be located
V31-23.exZh: No monitoring station has been set up in this neighbourhood.

V31-24.exZh: Priority will be given to residents living near the school.

V31-25.exZh: An independent team failed to replicate this result.

title: Reading I: informative articles
